title: Where it didn't

cards: Nobody makes a poster of this part. Three in the morning, a year into the practice, someone lies awake who knows all the lines by now. Some things are up to us, some aren't.
It isn't the thing, it's the judgment about the thing. They could recite them in their sleep, if they could sleep. And none of it is loosening the knot in the chest.
The words sit there like a poster on a waiting-room wall. Yesterday was where the porch helped. Today, just as plainly: where it didn't.

teach.h: SHOW ME A STOIC, IF YOU CAN.
teach.b: First, the Stoics saw this coming. In the Discourses, Epictetus challenges his students: show me a Stoic, if you can.

Not someone who can talk Stoic, but someone who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, disgraced and happy. He says he'd gladly see one, and implies he hasn't. And Marcus expects to be knocked out of tune.

When circumstances force you to be disturbed, he writes, come back to yourself quickly, and don't stay out of tune longer than you must. The teachers didn't claim the method always worked, even on them.
Second, where it can misfire. When it turns into small-s stoic: teeth gritted, feelings pushed down until they come out sideways.

When up to us and not up to us becomes an excuse to shrug at something you could change, or something unfair that someone should challenge. And when the trouble is depression, a deep loss, or a body that needs care.
A maxim is not a doctor, a friend, or a night's sleep. Third, two honest reasons. Sometimes the tool was fine and you were hungry, exhausted, or alone.
Sometimes it was the wrong tool for the job. Both are worth knowing, and neither is a failure of character. Fourth, why say it out loud.
A practice that only reports its wins turns into a sales pitch.
One that can say here, it didn't help stays a practice, something you use with open eyes.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism look honestly at where it hasn't helped, and pair it with other support, such as friends, counseling, rest or a faith community.

o: the emperor who wrote a private notebook to himself
the Roman who said the method never fails if done right
the teacher who asked to be shown even one true Stoic

games.q: honest about it — tap the pairs.
p: show me a Stoic, if you can
out of tune? come back quickly
a maxim is not a doctor

s: Epictetus said his school was full of finished Stoics
he challenged students to show him even one, and implied he hadn't seen one.
Marcus expected circumstances to shake him sometimes
Meditations 6.11 expects it, and tells him only to come back to himself quickly.
if Stoicism didn't help, you must have done it wrong
sometimes you were tired or alone; sometimes it was the wrong tool for the job.

games.q: you're one of Epictetus's students. he asks the room to show him one person who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, disgraced and happy. what happens?
o: he implies nobody there can show him one
games.why: Discourses 2.19: he says he'd gladly see such a Stoic, and the way he asks makes clear he hasn't yet. the teacher names the gap himself.

practice: Let one moment come where the porch didn't help, one you can look at today; you don't have to open the heaviest one. Ask gently: was I tired, hungry, alone, or was this the wrong tool?
If what comes up is heavy and still with you, that's a reason to talk to someone you trust, not to try harder alone.

wordCard.voice: Epictetus, who challenged his students to show him a Stoic who was sick and happy, in danger and happy, since the method doesn't always work, even on its teachers. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: honest about it. Naming the limits is part of the practice, not the end of it. Day six hundred ninety-four counts.
